short: A share with a very low price, usually of a tiny company, that trades rarely and can be pushed up or down easily.
kid: Some toys in the shop cost just one coin, but many of them break on the first day. A small price does not always mean a good deal.
detail: A penny stock is a share that trades at a very low price, typically of a company with a small market value and little analyst coverage. India has no legal definition; the term usually means shares priced in single digits or low double digits of rupees. In the US, SEC rules generally treat low-priced shares, roughly those under $5 that do not trade on a major exchange, as penny stocks and impose extra duties on brokers who sell them. Because few shares change hands, modest buying can send prices soaring, and selling can leave holders unable to exit. That makes them a favourite of pump-and-dump operators, and in India many sit under exchange surveillance such as the ASM framework. The key confusion: a low share price is not the same as cheap. Valuation depends on price relative to earnings, assets and cash flow, not on the rupee figure per share.
example: Say XYZ Ltd trades at ₹4 and earns ₹0.10 per share, so its P/E is 40. ABC Ltd trades at ₹2,000 and earns ₹100 per share, a P/E of 20. Per rupee of profit, the ₹4 penny stock is twice as expensive.

short: A stock whose price rises to several times what an investor paid for it, such as a ten-bagger that grows tenfold.
kid: You plant one little seed and it grows into a big tree full of fruit. You end up with many, many times more than you started with.
detail: A multibagger is an investment that returns several times its original cost. The word comes from baseball, where a 'bag' is a base: Peter Lynch popularised 'ten-bagger' in his 1989 book One Up on Wall Street for a stock that rises tenfold. Indian market media use 'multibagger' loosely for any stock that has doubled or more, often among small and mid-caps. Genuine multibaggers usually come from years of strong earnings growth combined with a rising valuation multiple, so patience and the ability to sit through deep falls matter more than spotting a hot tip. Two cautions. First, the label is applied with hindsight: for every past multibagger there are many similar-looking stocks that went nowhere or collapsed, a form of survivorship bias. Second, mind the arithmetic: a ten-bagger is a 900% gain, not 1,000%, because the gain is measured on top of the original money.
example: An investor buys 100 shares at ₹50, spending ₹5,000. If the price climbs to ₹500, the holding is worth ₹50,000, ten times the cost, so it is a ten-bagger. The gain is ₹45,000, or 900%.
formula: Multiple = Current value / Original cost; Percentage gain = (Multiple - 1) x 100

short: An investor stuck holding a stock that has fallen sharply, usually bought near the top, who keeps it hoping to break even.
kid: You swap your best sticker for a shiny new one, and then everyone stops liking shiny stickers. Now you are left holding something nobody wants.
detail: Bag holder is trading slang, popular on social-media forums, for someone left owning shares, tokens or other assets after the price has collapsed, often because they bought late in a hype-driven rally while earlier buyers sold to them. The bag holder usually keeps holding and waits to get back to the purchase price, instead of judging the asset on its prospects today. Behavioural finance explains why: loss aversion makes realising a loss painful, the disposition effect pushes people to sell winners and keep losers, and the purchase price acts as an anchor. In pump-and-dump schemes and meme-stock frenzies, creating bag holders is effectively the insiders' exit plan. The common confusion is treating holding on as long-term investing. Long-term investing is a deliberate view on a business; being a bag holder is avoiding a decision. The useful test is simple: would I buy this at today's price?
example: Say you bought 200 shares of XYZ Ltd at ₹300, paying ₹60,000. The price drops to ₹60, so the holding is worth ₹12,000, an 80% loss. Just to break even, the stock must now rise 400%, from ₹60 back to ₹300.
formula: Gain needed to break even = Loss / (1 - Loss), with the loss as a fraction (an 80% loss needs 0.8 / 0.2 = 4, i.e. a 400% gain)

short: An investor or trader so large that their buying or selling alone can move the price of a stock, coin or market.
kid: When a giant jumps into a swimming pool, water splashes everywhere. A whale is a giant in the money pool, and everyone feels the splash.
detail: A whale is a market participant whose positions are big enough to move prices by themselves: a large fund, a very wealthy individual, a corporate treasury or, in crypto, a wallet holding a large share of a coin's supply. The word is borrowed from casinos, where whales are the highest-stakes gamblers. Traders watch whales because one big sale can swamp the available buyers and drive prices down, while large purchases can spark rallies; crypto analysts even track whale wallets on public blockchains. Whale activity matters most in thinly traded assets, where the order book is shallow. A famous case is the 2012 'London Whale' episode, in which a JPMorgan Chase trader's outsized credit-derivative bets lost the bank about $6.2 billion. The common confusion: whales are not automatically smart money. Their size makes them visible and sometimes trapped, because exiting a huge position without crashing the price is hard.
example: Say a token has 1 billion units and one wallet holds 8% of them, or 80 million units. If only 20 million units trade on a normal day, the whale's stake equals four full days of trading, so dumping it quickly would almost certainly crash the price.

short: Money run by investors assumed to be better informed or more skilled, such as big institutions, company insiders and veteran traders.
kid: When the oldest kid in class picks a game, the others copy, because they think she knows best. She is not always right, though.
detail: Smart money refers to capital controlled by participants believed to have better information, research or experience: institutional investors, hedge funds, central banks, company insiders and seasoned traders. It is usually contrasted with 'dumb money', a dismissive label for small retail investors said to buy late and sell in panic. Investors try to follow smart money through disclosures: in India, bulk and block deal data, quarterly shareholding patterns and daily FII and DII flow figures; in the US, the quarterly 13F filings that managers with at least $100 million in qualifying US securities must submit. Watching large players can be informative, but the label is a stereotype, not a law. Institutions have herded into bubbles and been wrong at scale, as the 1998 collapse of the hedge fund Long-Term Capital Management showed, and disclosures arrive with a lag, so copying them means buying after the smart money has already moved.
example: Say a disclosure shows a large fund bought 5 lakh shares of ABC Ltd at ₹400, a ₹20 crore deal. Copycats pile in the next day at ₹440. If the price settles back to ₹400, they are down ₹40 a share, about 9.1%, while the fund is flat.

short: An illegal scheme in which fraudsters hype a cheap, rarely traded stock to push its price up, then sell their own shares to the buyers.
kid: A kid tells everyone his old marbles are magic, so friends rush to buy them. Once he has sold them all, everyone finds out they were just ordinary marbles.
detail: A pump and dump is a form of market manipulation. Operators first quietly accumulate a small, illiquid stock or crypto token at low prices, sometimes trading among linked accounts to fake activity. They then 'pump' it with misleading tips spread through Telegram and WhatsApp groups, bulk SMS, YouTube videos or paid finfluencers, promising huge gains. As retail buyers rush in and the price climbs, the operators 'dump' their holdings; the price then collapses and late buyers are left with heavy losses. In India, SEBI pursues such operator-driven stocks under its regulations against fraudulent and unfair trade practices, and exchanges place suspicious counters under surveillance. Warning signs include a sudden price surge with no news, unsolicited tips, a tiny free float and a run of upper circuits. The common confusion: a genuine rally on strong results is not a pump; manipulation requires deception.
example: Operators buy 50 lakh shares of a hypothetical XYZ Ltd at ₹10, spending ₹5 crore. After a tip campaign lifts the price to ₹40, they sell everything at an average of ₹35, collecting ₹17.5 crore, a ₹12.5 crore profit. The price then sinks to ₹8, leaving anyone who bought at ₹35 down about 77%.

short: A trading mistake caused by typing the wrong number, such as an extra zero in the quantity or price of an order.
kid: You meant to give your friend one sweet, but your hand slipped and you gave away the whole jar. Oops!
detail: A fat finger is a keying error in which a trader or investor enters the wrong quantity, price or instrument, for example selling 1,00,000 shares instead of 1,000, or typing a price with a misplaced decimal. With electronic and algorithmic trading, such orders execute in milliseconds and can jolt prices, trigger stop-losses and ripple across markets. A famous case: in December 2005 a Mizuho Securities trader meant to sell one J-Com share for ¥610,000 but entered 610,000 shares at ¥1, costing the firm about ¥40 billion. In India, erroneous orders worth about ₹650 crore placed through one broker on 5 October 2012 briefly knocked the Nifty down around 15% and halted trading. Exchanges and brokers now use price bands, order-value limits and quantity freezes to block such orders. The common confusion: a fat-finger move is an error, not a signal, so prices usually snap back once it is spotted.
example: A dealer means to sell 1,000 shares of ABC Ltd at ₹500, an order worth ₹5 lakh, but types 1,00,000 shares. The order is now worth ₹5 crore, 100 times larger, and could drag the price down sharply if there are not enough buyers waiting.

short: Making a portfolio or balance sheet look better just before a reporting date, through cosmetic moves that hide what really happened.
kid: Before your parents check your room, you push everything under the bed. The room looks tidy, but the mess is still there.
detail: Window dressing is cosmetic tidying ahead of a reporting date. For fund managers, it means buying the quarter's best-performing stocks and dumping the losers just before quarter-end or year-end, so the holdings list sent to investors looks smart. The returns already earned do not change, and the extra trading adds costs. A more aggressive variant, sometimes called portfolio pumping, involves heavy buying near the close to lift a holding's last price and the fund's reported value, which regulators treat as manipulation. Companies and banks can also window-dress balance sheets, for example by cutting borrowings just before the period ends and reversing it days later. Under SEBI rules as of 2025, Indian mutual funds disclose full portfolios at least monthly, so analysts compare successive disclosures and watch for unusual churn. The common confusion: window dressing is often legal but misleading; it becomes fraud when it involves false accounting or price manipulation.
example: A fund bought ₹50 crore of a stock that fell 30% during the quarter, to ₹35 crore. On the last trading day the manager sells it and buys a recent winner, so the month-end factsheet shows only winners. The ₹15 crore loss is already in the fund's value, and the extra trades only add costs.

short: The few weeks after each quarter ends when most listed companies publish their quarterly results.
kid: At the end of term, every child brings home a report card on almost the same few days. This is report-card time for companies.
detail: Earnings season is the cluster of weeks after each calendar quarter when most listed companies release their quarterly financial results, usually followed by earnings calls with analysts. In the US it begins about two weeks after quarter-end, traditionally with the big banks, and runs for roughly six weeks. In India, SEBI's listing rules as of 2025 require quarterly results within 45 days of the quarter's end and audited annual results within 60 days, so the season runs from mid-month into the following month, with large IT services companies often among the first to report. Markets turn more volatile because results, guidance and management commentary move individual stocks, and together they shift estimates of index earnings. The common confusion: what matters is less whether profit grew than how it compares with consensus estimates and what management says about the coming quarters.
example: For the quarter ending 30 June, a listed Indian company must publish results by 14 August, 45 days later, under SEBI's rules as of 2025. For the January-March quarter, which also carries the audited full-year numbers, the deadline stretches to 30 May, 60 days after 31 March.

short: A company's own forecast of its future revenue, profit, margins or other numbers, usually given as a range for the next quarter or year.
kid: Before your lemonade stand opens, you tell your friends you think you will sell about ten cups this week. That guess is your guidance.
detail: Guidance is management's public forecast of key numbers, such as revenue growth, operating margin, earnings per share or capital spending, for an upcoming quarter or financial year. It is usually a range and is updated over time: raised, cut, narrowed, reaffirmed or withdrawn. Because guidance anchors analysts' estimates, a change in it often moves the share price more than the latest quarter's actual results. In the US, Regulation FD requires such material information to reach all investors at once, not selected analysts privately. In India, practice varies: some companies, including several IT services firms, give annual revenue growth guidance, while many offer only qualitative commentary. Many companies worldwide withdrew guidance in 2020 when the pandemic made the future too uncertain. Common confusions: guidance is the company's forecast, not analysts' consensus, and it is unrelated to a central bank's forward guidance about interest rates.
example: Say ABC Ltd reported revenue of ₹2,000 crore in FY26 and guides for 8-10% growth in FY27, implying ₹2,160-2,200 crore. If it later narrows guidance to 9-10%, the range becomes ₹2,180-2,200 crore.
formula: Implied figure = Base-year figure x (1 + Guided growth rate)

short: The average of the forecasts made by the analysts who follow a company, for figures such as next quarter's profit or revenue.
kid: Five friends guess how many sweets are in a jar, and you pick the guess in the middle. That middle guess is what everyone roughly agrees on.
detail: A consensus estimate is the mean or median of analysts' forecasts for a company's earnings per share, revenue, EBITDA or another figure for a given period. Data providers such as LSEG, Bloomberg, FactSet and S&P Capital IQ collect forecasts from sell-side analysts and publish the consensus; the same idea applies to economists' forecasts for GDP or inflation. Consensus matters because markets price in expectations: when results arrive, the share price reacts to the gap between the actual number and consensus, not to growth alone. Investors also watch the spread of estimates, since wide disagreement signals uncertainty, and how consensus is revised over time. Common confusions: consensus is the analysts' view, not the company's own guidance; a few stale or extreme forecasts can skew the mean; and traders sometimes talk of an unofficial 'whisper number' that differs from the published consensus.
example: Five analysts forecast quarterly EPS for ABC Ltd of ₹10, ₹11, ₹12, ₹12 and ₹20. The mean is ₹65 / 5 = ₹13, while the median is ₹12; the single bullish ₹20 forecast pulls the mean ₹1 above the median.
formula: Consensus (mean) = Sum of analysts' forecasts / Number of analysts; some providers report the median instead

short: When a company's reported profit or revenue comes in higher than the average forecast of the analysts who follow it.
kid: Everyone thought you would sell five cups of lemonade, and you sold seven. You did better than people guessed.
detail: An earnings beat, or positive earnings surprise, happens when a company reports earnings per share, revenue or margins above the consensus estimate for the period, usually expressed as a surprise percentage. Beats tend to lift share prices because they suggest the business is doing better than the market had priced in. The reaction depends on the details: a beat driven by a one-off gain, a lower tax rate or cost cuts while revenue misses is lower quality than one driven by sales, and a beat paired with weaker guidance can still send a stock down. Beats are also more common than they sound: in a typical quarter roughly three in four S&P 500 companies beat EPS estimates, partly because managements steer expectations to a level they can clear. The most prized combination is a 'beat and raise': topping estimates while lifting guidance.
example: Consensus expects ABC Ltd to earn ₹20 per share this quarter, and it reports ₹22. That is a beat of ₹2, a surprise of +10%. If management also cuts next year's guidance, the shares may still fall.
formula: Earnings surprise (%) = (Actual EPS - Consensus EPS) / |Consensus EPS| x 100

short: When a company's reported profit or revenue comes in lower than the average forecast of the analysts who follow it.
kid: Everyone thought your lemonade stand would sell ten cups, but you sold only six. You did worse than people guessed.
detail: An earnings miss, or negative earnings surprise, occurs when reported earnings per share, revenue or margins fall short of the consensus estimate. Because beats are so common, investors often punish misses harder than they reward beats of the same size, especially for richly valued growth stocks whose prices already assume strong delivery. The reaction also depends on why the miss happened: a one-off charge, a delayed order or a currency swing may be forgiven, while slowing demand or shrinking margins, especially alongside lower guidance, can trigger rating downgrades and estimate cuts. A miss on profit with strong revenue and confident guidance can even see the stock rise. The common confusion: a miss does not mean profit fell. A company can grow profit 15% year on year and still miss if analysts expected 20%.
example: Analysts expected XYZ Ltd's quarterly profit to rise 20%, from ₹100 crore a year ago to ₹120 crore. It reports ₹115 crore: still 15% growth, but a miss of ₹5 crore, about 4.2% below consensus.
formula: Earnings surprise (%) = (Actual EPS - Consensus EPS) / |Consensus EPS| x 100; a negative result is a miss

short: An analyst's estimate of what a share should be worth, usually within the next 12 months, based on a valuation of the company.
kid: Your friend looks at your toy car and says that by next summer it will be worth five stickers. That guess about later is like a target price.
detail: A target price is the share price a research analyst expects a stock to reach over a set horizon, most commonly 12 months. It is usually derived from a valuation: forecast earnings multiplied by a chosen P/E multiple, a discounted cash flow model or a sum-of-the-parts. The gap between the target and the current price, the implied upside or downside, drives the analyst's rating. Investors use targets to compare brokers' views and gauge how much optimism is already in the price. Common confusions: a target price is an opinion, not a promise or a forecast for a specific date, and analysts often revise targets after the price has already moved, so targets can trail the market. It also differs from a trader's personal profit target on a position. In India, research analysts must be registered with SEBI and disclose conflicts of interest.
example: An analyst forecasts FY27 EPS of ₹50 for ABC Ltd and applies a P/E of 24, giving a target price of ₹1,200. With the stock at ₹1,000, the implied upside is 20%.
formula: Target price = Forecast EPS x Target P/E (one common method); Implied upside = (Target price - Current price) / Current price

short: A research analyst's recommendation on a stock, such as buy, hold or sell, based on how much it is expected to gain or lose.
kid: A friend tries every flavour of ice cream and tells you: get this one, this one is okay, skip that one. That advice is like a rating.
detail: An analyst rating is a sell-side research analyst's recommendation on a stock. Labels vary by firm: buy, hold and sell; outperform, neutral and underperform; overweight, equal-weight and underweight; and at many Indian brokerages also accumulate, add and reduce. Each firm defines its own scale, either by expected absolute return over about 12 months or by expected performance against a benchmark or sector, so the same word can mean different things at two brokers. Ratings and target prices move stocks, particularly when a widely followed analyst changes a call. Common confusions: ratings are skewed heavily towards buy, sell ratings are rare, and a hold can quietly signal caution. Analysts can also face conflicts of interest from their firm's banking ties, which is why SEBI's research analyst regulations and similar rules abroad require disclosures. A rating is one input, not personal advice suited to your goals.
example: Say a broker rates a stock Buy if its expected 12-month return exceeds 15%, Hold between -5% and 15%, and Sell below -5%. With the stock at ₹800 and a target of ₹960, the expected return is 20%, so Buy. If the price rises to ₹900 with no change in target, the expected return drops to about 6.7% and the rating becomes Hold.
formula: Expected return = (Target price - Current price) / Current price, plus any expected dividend yield

short: When an analyst raises their recommendation on a stock, for example from hold to buy, signalling a more positive view.
kid: Your friend used to say your drawing was just okay, and now says it is great. Their opinion went up a step.
detail: In equity news, an upgrade is a research analyst raising a stock's rating, such as from sell to hold or hold to buy, usually with a higher target price and a note explaining why: better earnings prospects, an attractive valuation after a fall, or an improving industry. A jump of two steps, from sell to buy, is called a double upgrade. Upgrades from influential brokers can lift a stock on the day, especially mid and small caps with few analysts. Read the reasoning, not just the headline: an upgrade on valuation alone after a sharp drop sends a different message from one driven by rising earnings estimates. Do not confuse it with three neighbours: a credit rating upgrade by an agency such as CRISIL or Moody's, which concerns default risk on debt; an earnings upgrade, which is a higher profit forecast; and a re-rating, which is a higher valuation multiple.
example: An analyst moves ABC Ltd from Hold to Buy and lifts the target price from ₹500 to ₹600. With the stock at ₹480, the implied upside rises from about 4.2% to 25%.

short: When an analyst lowers their recommendation on a stock, for example from buy to hold or sell, signalling a more cautious view.
kid: Your friend used to say your sandcastle was the best, and now says it is only okay. Their opinion went down a step.
detail: A downgrade is a research analyst cutting a stock's rating, such as from buy to hold or from hold to sell, often with a lower target price. Typical reasons are weaker earnings prospects, rising competition, governance worries or a valuation that has run ahead of fundamentals. Moving two steps, from buy to sell, is a double downgrade and tends to make headlines. Because sell ratings are rare, even a downgrade to hold can be a meaningful warning. Read the reason: a valuation downgrade after a big rise says the price looks full, not that the business is in trouble. Keep three terms apart: a credit rating downgrade by agencies such as CRISIL or S&P, which concerns default risk on debt; an earnings downgrade, which is a lower profit forecast; and a de-rating, a fall in the valuation multiple.
example: An analyst cuts XYZ Ltd from Buy to Sell, a double downgrade, and lowers the target from ₹900 to ₹700. With the stock at ₹800, the implied return swings from +12.5% to -12.5%.

short: The street in Mumbai where the BSE stands, and a nickname for India's stock market and its investors as a whole.
kid: Sometimes people call a whole place by the name of one famous street. Dalal Street is the street people name when they mean the big place where India buys and sells tiny pieces of companies.
detail: Dalal Street is a road in Mumbai's Fort area that houses BSE, formerly the Bombay Stock Exchange, in the Phiroze Jeejeebhoy Towers. 'Dalal' means broker in Hindi and Marathi. Share brokers who once met under banyan trees near the Town Hall moved to the street in the 1870s, and their association, formed in 1875, grew into BSE, often described as Asia's oldest stock exchange. Today the name is shorthand for the Indian equity market and its investors, much as Wall Street stands for American finance: 'Dalal Street rallies' means the Sensex and Nifty rose, and 'investors richer by ₹3 lakh crore' refers to a rise in total market capitalisation. The common confusion: the National Stock Exchange, where most Indian equity trading now happens, is not on Dalal Street but in the Bandra Kurla Complex. The nickname covers both exchanges.
example: A headline says 'Dalal Street investors richer by ₹3 lakh crore'. Say the total market capitalisation of BSE-listed companies rose from ₹400 lakh crore to ₹403 lakh crore that day: the ₹3 lakh crore gain is 0.75% of the starting value.

short: A street in New York where the New York Stock Exchange stands, and a nickname for America's financial markets and big banks.
kid: Wall Street is a real street in a big city. People use its name to mean all the grown-ups there who buy and sell little pieces of companies.
detail: Wall Street is a street in Lower Manhattan, named after a wooden wall built by the Dutch settlers of New Amsterdam in the 17th century. The New York Stock Exchange traces its origins to the 1792 Buttonwood Agreement among brokers nearby and stands at 11 Wall Street. In the news, Wall Street means the US financial industry and markets collectively: 'Wall Street closes lower' means the main US indices fell. 'The Street' is related shorthand for sell-side analysts as a group, as in 'beat Street estimates'. Because US markets are the world's largest and set the tone for global risk appetite, Indian traders check Wall Street's overnight moves before the local open. The common confusion: the term is a label rather than an address; the Nasdaq is based in Times Square, and most big banks have their headquarters away from Wall Street, some outside New York altogether.
example: If a news line reads 'Wall Street ends lower; S&P 500 falls 1.5%', a $10,000 holding in an S&P 500 index fund would be worth about $9,850 at that day's close.

short: A nickname for ordinary households, workers and small businesses, used to contrast the everyday economy with financial markets and big banks.
kid: Main Street is where the corner shop, the baker and the barber work. It means everyday people, not the big money traders.
detail: Main Street is American shorthand for ordinary people and small businesses, the everyday economy of jobs, wages and shops, as opposed to Wall Street, the world of investment banks, traders and share prices. The contrast is common in policy debates: critics of the 2008 bank bailouts asked why Wall Street was rescued while Main Street lost homes and jobs, and in 2020 the US Federal Reserve set up a Main Street Lending Program for small and mid-sized firms. Markets and the real economy can diverge. Stock indices reflect the expected future profits of large listed companies, interest rates and global money flows, while Main Street feels today's unemployment, prices and access to credit. In 2020, US stocks hit record highs while unemployment was still high. The common confusion: a rising stock market does not mean most households or small businesses are doing well, and vice versa.
example: Say in one year a stock index rises 20% while small-shop sales fall 5%. An investor with $10,000 in an index fund gains $2,000, while a shop with $200,000 in annual sales loses $10,000 of revenue: Wall Street up, Main Street down.

short: Another word for a stock exchange, the marketplace where shares and other securities are bought and sold; common in news headlines.
kid: A bourse is a big market, like a busy bazaar. Instead of fruit, people there buy and sell small pieces of companies.
detail: Bourse is a French-derived word for a stock exchange, widely used in financial journalism, especially in headlines where it saves space: 'Asian bourses slip', 'the Mumbai bourse', 'Gulf bourses mixed'. The name is traditionally traced to the Van der Beurse family of medieval Bruges, in present-day Belgium, whose inn was a meeting place for merchants trading bills and goods; Antwerp, Paris and other cities later built formal bourses. Today the word covers any organised securities exchange, such as BSE and NSE in India or Euronext in Europe, and sometimes commodity exchanges. In Indian news, 'the bourses' usually means BSE and NSE together, and 'informed the bourses' means a company filed a disclosure with both exchanges. The common confusion: a bourse is the marketplace, not the index; 'the Mumbai bourse rose' really means its benchmark index, such as the Sensex, rose.
example: A headline reads 'Mumbai bourse's Sensex gains 0.8%'. An investor holding ₹1,00,000 in a Sensex index fund would see it worth about ₹1,00,800 that day, before costs.

short: An Indian way of writing big numbers: one lakh crore is 1,00,000 crore, which equals one trillion (10 to the power 12).
kid: In India, people use special words, lakh and crore, for very big numbers. A lakh crore is so big that if you counted one number every second, you could never finish in your whole life.
detail: India counts large numbers in lakhs and crores rather than millions and billions. One lakh is 1,00,000 (one hundred thousand) and one crore is 1,00,00,000 (ten million), which is 100 lakh. A lakh crore is therefore 1,00,000 crore, or 10^12: one trillion. Indian commas follow the same system, grouping digits in twos after the first three, so ten million is written 1,00,00,000 rather than 10,000,000. Lakh crore is the natural unit for national totals such as the Union Budget, GDP, bank deposits, market capitalisation and government borrowing, so it appears constantly in Indian financial news. Common mistakes: confusing ₹1 lakh crore with ₹1 billion (it is 1,000 times larger), dropping a zero when converting, and quoting a rupee figure in dollars without saying which exchange rate was used. Because the rupee moves, any dollar conversion should name the rate it assumes.
example: A company valued at ₹20 lakh crore is worth ₹20 trillion, or 20 x 10^12 rupees. At an assumed rate of ₹85 per dollar, that is about $235 billion. Going the other way, ₹1 crore is ₹10 million, so ₹100 crore is ₹1 billion.
formula: 1 lakh = 1,00,000 = 10^5; 1 crore = 100 lakh = 10^7; 1 lakh crore = 1,00,000 crore = 10^12 (one trillion)

short: A stock whose price soars because of hype and coordinated buying by small investors on social media, rather than because of the company's business.
kid: One day everyone at school suddenly wants the same plain pencil because it became a funny joke. The pencil is not any better; it is just popular for a while.
detail: A meme stock is a share that goes viral online and attracts a flood of retail buying driven by social-media posts and jokes, often regardless of the company's earnings. The defining episode came in January 2021, when users of Reddit's WallStreetBets forum piled into GameStop, a struggling video-game retailer heavily shorted by hedge funds. Heavy buying of shares and call options forced short sellers to buy back stock in a short squeeze, and GameStop rose from under $20 at the start of the month to an intraday peak of $483 on 28 January, before a later four-for-one split. AMC Entertainment and others followed. Meme rallies can make early buyers rich, but prices tend to collapse once attention moves on, leaving late buyers with large losses. The common confusion: popularity is not value; a meme rally says more about crowd psychology and market mechanics than about the business.
example: Say online buying lifts a hypothetical XYZ Inc from $10 to $80 in two weeks, a 700% rise. A trader who buys at $80 and holds as the price slides back to $20 loses 75% of the money invested.

short: Selling investments in a hurry, at almost any price, out of fear that prices will keep falling, rather than after careful thought.
kid: Someone shouts that the ice cream is melting, so everyone rushes to give theirs away. Later they find out it was fine all along.
detail: Panic selling is a wave of selling driven by fear rather than analysis: investors rush to get out and accept ever-lower prices, which pushes prices down further and frightens more holders into selling. It is usually set off by a shock and amplified by margin calls, stop-loss orders and fund redemptions that force selling. Famous examples include Black Monday, 19 October 1987, when the Dow fell 22.6% in a day, and March 2020, when Indian indices hit the 10% market-wide circuit breaker twice and the Sensex fell about 13% on 23 March alone. Exchanges use circuit breakers to pause trading and let panic cool. A related term, fire sale, means forced selling of assets well below fair value because the seller urgently needs cash. The common confusion: selling in a panic locks in losses, and the sharpest rebounds often come soon after the worst days.
example: Say an investor's ₹5 lakh portfolio falls 30% to ₹3.5 lakh and they sell in fear. If the market then rebounds 40% from that low, the portfolio would have recovered to ₹4.9 lakh: selling locked in a ₹1.5 lakh loss and missed a ₹1.4 lakh rebound.

short: A price move that looks like the start of a rise, tempting traders to buy, before the price turns and falls again.
kid: The sun peeks out, so you leave your umbrella at home, and then it pours again. The sunshine tricked you.
detail: A bull trap is a false signal that a falling or sideways price has turned up: the price breaks above a resistance level or bounces sharply, drawing in buyers, then reverses lower and traps them in losses. Its mirror image, a bear trap, is a false breakdown below a support level that lures sellers and short sellers before the price snaps back up, sometimes forcing shorts to buy back in a squeeze. Both terms come from technical analysis. Traders try to avoid traps by waiting for confirmation, such as a close above the level on strong volume, and by using stop-loss orders. In long bear markets, short bursts of rising prices are often bull traps. The common confusion: a trap is only clear in hindsight. No pattern reliably separates a real breakout from a false one in advance, which is why risk control matters more than prediction.
example: ABC Ltd has been capped at ₹500 for months, then jumps to ₹520 on light volume. A trader buys 100 shares at ₹515, but within a week the price falls back to ₹470. The trader is down ₹45 a share, or ₹4,500 in total, about 8.7%.

short: A 2025 market nickname for buying after a Trump tariff threat knocks prices down, betting the threat will be softened or delayed.
kid: A big kid keeps saying he will take everyone's toys, then changes his mind. After a while, the other kids stop getting scared and just keep playing.
detail: TACO stands for 'Trump Always Chickens Out', a phrase coined in May 2025 by Financial Times columnist Robert Armstrong. It describes a 2025 pattern: President Donald Trump announced steep tariffs or threats, markets fell, then the measures were paused, delayed or watered down and markets rebounded. The clearest example followed the sweeping 'Liberation Day' tariffs of 2 April 2025: when a 90-day pause on the higher country-specific rates, for every country except China, was announced on 9 April, the S&P 500 jumped about 9.5% in a day. The TACO trade means buying such dips, expecting a reversal. Its risks are real: a threat may stick, and if markets treat a climbdown as certain, the market pain that helped prompt past reversals may not arrive. The common confusion: it is a nickname for an observed pattern, not an official term or a reliable strategy, and political patterns can break without warning.
example: Say an index drops 10% in a week on a tariff threat, from 5,000 to 4,500. A trader buys at 4,500, and when the tariffs are delayed the index climbs to 4,950, a 10% gain on the purchase. Had the tariffs stuck and the index fallen to 4,050, the trader would have lost 10%.

short: Buying assets such as gold, silver or bitcoin as protection against government currencies steadily losing their purchasing power.
kid: If every week your pocket money buys fewer sweets, you might swap it for marbles that do not shrink. That swap is the idea here.
detail: The debasement trade is an investment theme built on the fear that major currencies, especially the US dollar, will lose purchasing power because governments run large deficits, public debt keeps rising and central banks may be pressured to hold rates down or create money. Investors respond by buying assets whose supply policymakers cannot expand at will, such as gold, silver and bitcoin, while avoiding long-dated government bonds. The term echoes history, when rulers cut the precious-metal content of coins, as in ancient Rome or Henry VIII's 'Great Debasement' of the 1540s. The theme drew wide attention in 2025 as gold set repeated record highs amid worries over US fiscal policy and the Federal Reserve's independence. The common confusion: debasement means gradual erosion, not hyperinflation, and the trade is a narrative; gold and bitcoin can still fall sharply when real interest rates rise or fear fades.
example: If a currency loses 3% of its purchasing power every year, $100,000 held in cash buys only what about $73,700 bought originally after 10 years, because 0.97 raised to the 10th power is about 0.737.
formula: Real value after n years = Amount x (1 - Annual loss of purchasing power)^n

short: Investors selling US shares, US government bonds and the dollar at the same time because of doubts about American policy and safety.
kid: The most popular shop in town suddenly keeps changing its rules, so some shoppers take their money to other shops for a while.
detail: The Sell America trade describes episodes when US stocks, long-dated Treasury bonds and the dollar all fall together. That combination is unusual: in most sell-offs, Treasuries and the dollar rise because investors treat them as safe havens. It came to prominence in April 2025, after the sweeping 'Liberation Day' tariffs, when long-term Treasury yields rose sharply and the dollar weakened even as stocks slid. Drivers cited include unpredictable trade policy, large fiscal deficits, pressure on the Federal Reserve's independence and Moody's cut of the US from its top Aaa rating in May 2025. The dollar index had its weakest first half since the early 1970s. The trade is also framed as an unwinding of 'US exceptionalism', the long run of US outperformance. The common confusion: it rarely means a wholesale exodus; much of it reflects foreign investors hedging dollar exposure rather than dumping everything.
example: A European investor holds $100,000 of US shares bought when €1 = $1.05, so they cost about €95,238. If the shares fall 5% to $95,000 and the dollar weakens to €1 = $1.15, the holding is worth about €82,609: a loss of roughly 13.3% in euros, though the shares fell only 5%.

short: Investing in companies expected to profit from artificial intelligence, such as chipmakers, cloud giants and data-centre suppliers, and the market rally around them.
kid: When everyone wants a new kind of toy robot, the shops that make robot parts get very busy. People rush to own a piece of those shops.
detail: The AI trade is the market theme of buying companies seen as winners from artificial intelligence. It took off after OpenAI released ChatGPT in November 2022 and centres on chip designers and makers such as Nvidia, TSMC and Broadcom; cloud 'hyperscalers' such as Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon and Meta that spend heavily on data centres; and suppliers of memory, networking, power and cooling. It has driven much of the US market's gains, concentrated indices in a few giant stocks and in July 2025 made Nvidia the first company valued at $4 trillion. Few listed Indian companies are direct AI plays. Bulls point to real revenue growth; sceptics warn of an 'AI bubble' like the dot-com era and question whether huge capital spending will pay off. The common confusion: a transformative technology can still be a poor investment if buyers overpay.
example: Say a hypothetical chipmaker earns $10 billion a year and the market values it at 50 times earnings, or $500 billion. If AI enthusiasm cools and investors will pay only 25 times, its value halves to $250 billion even though profit has not fallen at all.

short: How willing investors as a group are, at a given moment, to take chances with their money; it rises and falls with news and fear.
kid: On a sunny day, kids happily try the tall slide. On a stormy day, they stay on the small swings. How brave they feel changes with the weather.
detail: Risk appetite is the market's collective willingness to hold riskier assets, such as equities, high-yield bonds, emerging-market assets and crypto, rather than safer ones such as cash, government bonds and gold. When it is strong, a 'risk-on' mood, investors accept thinner rewards for taking risk, credit spreads narrow and money flows into emerging markets such as India. When it weakens, a 'risk-off' move, investors demand more compensation, spreads widen, volatility gauges such as the VIX and India VIX jump, the US dollar often strengthens and foreign portfolio investors tend to pull money out of Indian shares. Shifts are driven by growth data, central-bank decisions, geopolitics and sudden shocks. The common confusion: risk appetite describes the whole market's mood at a point in time, while risk tolerance and risk aversion usually describe an individual investor's lasting ability and willingness to bear losses.
example: Say that when risk appetite is strong, investors buy a junk bond yielding 8% while Treasuries yield 4%, a spread of 4 percentage points. In a risk-off scare, the same bond may need to yield 11% to find buyers while Treasuries still yield 4%, so the spread widens to 7 points.

short: Buying a stock while its price is crashing, hoping it has hit bottom, at the risk that it keeps on falling.
kid: If a glass is falling off the table, grabbing it in mid-air can hurt your hand. It is safer to wait until it has landed.
detail: Catching a falling knife means buying an asset during a steep, fast decline in the hope of getting it near the bottom. The saying warns that, just as grabbing a falling knife is likely to hurt, buying too early in a crash often leads to further losses, because sharp falls frequently reflect real problems such as fraud, a broken business model, heavy debt or forced selling that has not finished. Bottom fishing is the gentler, related term for hunting for bargains among beaten-down stocks. Careful investors try to tell the two apart by asking whether the cause of the fall is temporary or permanent, waiting for the price to stabilise, and buying in stages rather than all at once. The common confusion: a big fall does not make a stock cheap. A share that is down 50% can halve again, and value traps look like bargains all the way down.
example: An investor buys XYZ Ltd at ₹200 after it has fallen 50% from ₹400. It then halves again to ₹100. The buyer has lost 50%, the stock is down 75% from its peak, and it must now double just to get back to ₹200.

short: An early announcement by a company, before its scheduled results, that profit will come in well below what it or the market expected.
kid: Before report-card day, you tell your parents your marks will be lower than you hoped. Telling them early is a warning.
detail: A profit warning is a statement, usually in an unscheduled trading update, that a company's profit for the current period will fall materially short of its guidance or of market expectations. It is common in the UK and Europe, where listed companies must disclose price-sensitive information as soon as possible; in the US it is often called a negative pre-announcement. Typical causes include weaker demand, cost overruns, lost contracts or currency swings. Shares often fall sharply because analysts cut forecasts and investors question management's credibility, and many speak of a 'cockroach' effect: one warning is often followed by more. Indian companies issue formal profit warnings less often, though material developments must be disclosed to the exchanges under SEBI's listing rules. The common confusion: a profit warning is not the same as an earnings miss; the warning comes before the results, while a miss is judged when results are published.
example: Say ABC Inc guided for full-year profit of $100 million. Partway through the year it warns that profit will be about $80 million, 20% lower, and its shares fall from $40 to $30, a 25% drop, as analysts cut their forecasts.

short: A quarter in which a company books every possible loss, write-down and provision at once, so later results look better by comparison.
kid: When you finally clean your messy room, you throw out every broken toy in one go. It looks bad that day, but your room stays tidy afterwards.
detail: A kitchen-sink quarter, also called taking a big bath, is a reporting period in which management recognises as many bad items as possible at once: asset impairments, goodwill write-downs, restructuring costs, extra provisions for doubtful loans and inventory write-offs. It often follows a change of CEO or a failed acquisition: markets tend to punish one terrible quarter less than a string of disappointments, and new managers can blame their predecessors. It also lowers the base for future comparisons, and generous provisions can later be released back into profit, flattering results. Indian banks' large bad-loan recognition after the RBI's 2015 asset quality review is often described in these terms, though that clean-up was regulator-driven. The common confusion: a kitchen-sink quarter can be an honest reset or a form of earnings management; investors should check whether provisions are later written back and whether the losses were real.
example: A new CEO at a hypothetical ABC Ltd books ₹600 crore of impairments and provisions in one quarter, turning an expected ₹200 crore profit into a ₹400 crore loss. Next year, a profit of ₹300 crore, including ₹50 crore of those provisions written back, is reported as a sharp turnaround.

short: Having your own money at risk in a decision you make or recommend, so you share the gains and the losses with others.
kid: If you bake a cake for your friends, you eat a slice too. If it tastes bad, you find out as well.
detail: Skin in the game means that the people making decisions, or giving advice, have their own money exposed to the outcome, so their incentives line up with investors'. Examples include promoters with large stakes, fund managers investing their own savings in their schemes, private equity partners committing capital alongside clients, and executives paid in shares that vest over years. It addresses the agency problem, in which managers who risk only other people's money may take too much risk or chase fees. In India, under SEBI rules as of 2025, part of the pay of key mutual fund employees must be invested in units of the schemes they oversee, with a lock-in. The phrase was popularised by Nassim Nicholas Taleb's 2018 book of that name. The common confusion: ownership aligns incentives but does not guarantee good decisions, and pledged promoter shares can shrink the real skin in the game.
example: A fund manager puts ₹50 lakh of her own savings into the ₹500 crore fund she runs. If the fund falls 10%, investors as a group lose ₹50 crore and she personally loses ₹5 lakh, so she feels the same pain they do.

short: Holding more (overweight) or less (underweight) of a stock, sector or country than its share of a benchmark index; also used as analyst ratings.
kid: Your class shares crayons so everyone gets the same of each colour. If you take extra blue and fewer red, you have more blue than usual and less red.
detail: Overweight and underweight describe a position relative to a benchmark. If banks make up 30% of a fund's benchmark index and the fund holds 36% in banks, it is overweight banks by 6 percentage points; holding 24% would make it underweight. Equal-weight, or neutral, means matching the benchmark. Fund managers and strategists use the terms for stocks, sectors, countries and asset classes, as in 'global investors are overweight India' or 'we turn underweight bonds'. Several brokers, such as Morgan Stanley, also use Overweight, Equal-weight and Underweight as stock ratings, meaning the analyst expects the stock to beat, match or lag its sector or coverage group, typically over about 12 months. The common confusions: overweight does not mean the stock is the fund's largest holding, and underweight does not mean selling everything; an underweight fund can still own plenty of the stock, just less than the index does.
example: Say financials are 30% of a fund's benchmark and the fund holds 36%, an overweight of 6 percentage points. If financial stocks then beat the benchmark by 10%, that overweight adds about 0.6 percentage points to the fund's relative return (6% x 10%).
formula: Active weight = Portfolio weight - Benchmark weight (positive = overweight, negative = underweight)

short: A change by analysts to their forecast of a company's future profit, either raised (an upgrade) or lowered (a downgrade or cut).
kid: You guess you will collect ten shells at the beach, but after an hour you change your guess to fifteen. Changing your guess is a revision.
detail: An earnings revision is a change to analysts' forecasts of a company's earnings per share, or of an index's combined earnings, for future periods. Upgrades raise estimates; downgrades or cuts lower them. Revisions follow results, guidance changes, commodity and currency moves, or shifts in demand. They matter because share prices are tied to expected future profits: if estimates fall while the P/E multiple stays the same, fair value falls with them. Research has long found an estimate-revision or earnings-momentum effect, in which stocks with rising estimates tend to keep outperforming for a while, partly because analysts adjust gradually. Indian brokerages regularly report how much they have cut or raised their Nifty EPS forecasts after each results season. The common confusion: an earnings downgrade changes the profit forecast, while an analyst downgrade changes the stock's rating. They often arrive together but are different things.
example: An analyst cuts the FY27 EPS forecast for ABC Ltd from ₹80 to ₹72, a 10% downgrade. At an unchanged P/E of 20, the implied fair value falls from ₹1,600 to ₹1,440.
formula: Revision (%) = (New EPS estimate - Old EPS estimate) / Old EPS estimate x 100; Revision ratio = (Upgrades - Downgrades) / Total number of estimate changes

short: A fraud that pays earlier investors with money taken from newer investors, instead of from real profits, until new money runs out.
kid: A boy says he can grow sweets. He takes sweets from new friends to give to old friends, and when no new friends come, everyone learns he never grew any.
detail: A Ponzi scheme is an investment fraud that promises high, steady returns but has little or no genuine business: the operator pays existing investors out of deposits from new ones, and the illusion survives only while fresh money arrives faster than withdrawals. It is named after Charles Ponzi, who ran a postal-coupon scheme in Boston in 1920. The largest known case is Bernard Madoff's, exposed in December 2008, with paper losses of about $65 billion. India has seen many, including the collapse of the Saradha group's schemes in 2013; SEBI regulates collective investment schemes, and the Banning of Unregulated Deposit Schemes Act, 2019 outlaws unregistered deposit-taking. Warning signs: guaranteed high returns, unusually smooth performance, secrecy and pressure to reinvest. A pyramid scheme is related but distinct: participants earn mainly by recruiting others who pay to join, while in a Ponzi the central operator pays everyone.
example: Say a scheme collects ₹10 crore and promises 5% a month. That means ₹50 lakh of payouts every month with no real earnings, so after 20 months it has paid out the entire ₹10 crore and must keep raising fresh money just to stay afloat.
